title: Check a Relevant Baseline Before Interpreting One Case
subtitle: Put a vivid example beside the broader reference class it belongs to.
description: For an ordinary data-informed decision, define the relevant reference class, find a comparable baseline, inspect its scope and denominator, then combine that general context with the facts that are specific to the case.

lifeOsSource.hack: Before letting one memorable case define what you expect, identify the broader group of comparable cases and inspect the baseline that belongs to that group.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: State the decision, define the reference class, find a baseline with a clear denominator and scope, check whether it is comparable to the current case, add the case-specific information that genuinely differs, and keep the conclusion tentative when the baseline or fit is weak.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: What reference class did I use, where did its baseline come from, how comparable is it to this case, and which case-specific fact could justify departing from it?

faq.question: What makes a baseline relevant?
faq.answer: It should describe a group that is meaningfully comparable to the case and use a denominator that matches the question. A broad number from a different population, period, product, process or operating environment may be less useful than a narrower local record.
faq.answerHtml: It should describe a group that is meaningfully comparable to the case and use a denominator that matches the question. A broad number from a different population, period, product, process or operating environment may be less useful than a narrower local record.

faq.question: Should the baseline override specific information?
faq.answer: No. Use the baseline as context, then account for case-specific information that is relevant and reliable. The purpose is to prevent one vivid detail from silently replacing the broader context, not to ignore real differences.

faq.question: Can I use this for medical, legal or other high-stakes decisions?
faq.answer: This page is not a decision rule for high-stakes domains. Use domain-appropriate authoritative information and qualified professional guidance where required; a generic reference-class exercise is not a substitute for that review.

intro.html: A memorable example is information about one case. A baseline describes a broader set of cases. When a decision depends on what usually happens, put those two layers beside each other: define the reference class, inspect the baseline and its scope, then ask whether the current case contains information that should move the judgment away from that starting context.

sections.title: 1. Define the question and reference class
sections.html: State what you are trying to estimate or compare. Then define the group of cases that would make a meaningful baseline: the same type of task, customer, incident, product, project, process, or other relevant category.

sections.title: 2. Find a baseline with visible scope
sections.html: Record where the baseline comes from, what period and population it covers, and what denominator it uses. If you cannot identify those basics, treat the number or frequency as weak context rather than a precise anchor.

sections.title: 3. Check whether the baseline fits this case
sections.html: Compare the current case with the reference class. Note differences that could matter, such as a changed process, environment, segment, requirement or selection rule. Do not borrow precision from a baseline that describes a materially different situation.

sections.title: 4. Combine general context with specific facts
sections.html: Use the baseline as starting context and add the information that is genuinely specific to the case. If the reference class is weak or the specific information is incomplete, keep the decision reversible where possible and state what remains unknown.

editorialCuration.reason: Replace unsupported accuracy claims, fabricated outcomes, arbitrary sample-size confidence rules and medical, political, hiring and relationship prescriptions with a bounded reference-class and applicability workflow.
